items.prompt: Your skin and the lining of your airways stop most germs from getting in. What role do they play?

options.label: A first line of defense most germs cannot cross
A second layer that learns each new germ
A store of antibodies kept for later use
A factory that makes new white blood cells

items.explain: Epithelial surfaces form a physical barrier that is impermeable to most infectious agents, acting as the first line of defense.

items.prompt: Your eyes water and your mouth stays moist. How do tears and saliva help protect you?

options.label: By teaching T cells to recognize germs
By hardening the skin
By flushing away infectious agents
By clotting the blood

items.explain: The flushing action of tears and saliva helps prevent infection of the eyes and mouth.

items.prompt: How can the normal bacteria living in your gut keep a harmful bacterium from settling in?

options.label: By building antibodies against it
By competing with it for nutrients and attachment sites
By vaccinating the gut wall
By shedding the skin that covers it

items.explain: Gut flora can prevent colonization by pathogens by secreting toxic substances or by competing for nutrients or cell surface attachment sites.

items.prompt: A biologist studies how a fungus defends itself against infection. Which immune strategy is the dominant one in it?

options.label: The adaptive strategy
The antibody strategy
The vaccine strategy
The innate strategy

items.explain: The innate immune system is the dominant response found in plants, fungi, prokaryotes, and invertebrates.

items.prompt: Inflammation puts up a physical barrier against infection spreading. What else does it do?

options.label: It promotes healing of damaged tissue
It builds an immunological memory
It makes new antibodies
It sheds the outer skin

items.explain: Inflammation establishes a physical barrier against the spread of infection and promotes healing of damaged tissue after the pathogen is cleared.

items.prompt: Where does the alarm that starts acute inflammation come from?

options.label: Antibodies delivered in by the bone marrow
Cells already in tissues, such as macrophages and mast cells
T cells that were produced after a first exposure
Vaccines that were given before the infection

items.explain: Acute inflammation is initiated by cells already present in all tissues, mainly resident macrophages, dendritic cells, histiocytes, Kupffer cells, and mast cells.

paragraphs.heading: The non-specific defense
paragraphs.text: The innate immune system, also called the non-specific immune system, is the dominant immune response in plants, fungi, prokaryotes and invertebrates. In vertebrates it is one of two main immunity strategies, the other being the adaptive immune system, and it has been studied most in vertebrates. It acts as a physical and chemical barrier, through skin and mucus as well as clotting factors and host defence peptides. It also starts and regulates inflammation by releasing inflammatory mediators such as cytokines and chemokines, which draw immune cells to sites of infection.

paragraphs.heading: Barriers at the surface
paragraphs.text: Epithelial surfaces form a physical barrier that most infectious agents cannot pass, making them the first line of defense. The skin's epithelium sheds, which helps remove bacteria stuck to it. The epidermis has no blood vessels and cannot hold moisture, and the dermis has sebaceous glands, so microbes find it a poor place to survive. In the gut, peristalsis moves infectious agents along, cilia do the same in the airways, and mucus traps them. Tears and saliva flush the eyes and mouth, and gut flora block harmful bacteria by releasing toxic substances or competing for nutrients and attachment sites.

paragraphs.heading: A newer idea about barriers
paragraphs.text: The epithelial barrier hypothesis suggests that damage to these barriers by toxic substances in the environment, such as detergents, air pollutants, microplastics, food additives and nanoparticles, helps bring on chronic diseases. Immunologist Cezmi Akdis first framed it in the early 2020s to explain the growing number of chronic inflammatory diseases in industrialized societies. Conditions it has been linked to include asthma, atopic dermatitis, food allergy and type 1 diabetes. Critics point out that many of these links are still correlations and call for long-term human studies.

paragraphs.heading: Inflammation
paragraphs.text: Inflammation is one of the immune system's first responses to infection or irritation, and it is set off by chemical factors released from injured cells. It forms a physical barrier against the spread of infection and helps damaged tissue heal after the pathogen is cleared. Acute inflammation is started by cells that sit in every tissue, chiefly resident macrophages along with mast cells, dendritic cells, Kupffer cells and histiocytes. These carry pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs): molecules widely shared by pathogens but different from the host's own.

paragraphs.heading: Raising the alarm
paragraphs.text: When one of a cell's PRRs recognizes a PAMP, the cell is activated and releases cytokines and chemokines, which cause the clinical signs of inflammation. Other chemicals made during inflammation, including histamine, bradykinin, serotonin, leukotrienes and prostaglandins, sensitize pain receptors, widen nearby blood vessels and attract phagocytes, especially neutrophils. Neutrophils then bring in more of the immune system by releasing factors that summon further leukocytes and lymphocytes. Cytokines made by macrophages and other innate cells, such as TNF, HMGB1 and IL-1, drive the inflammatory response.

paragraphs.heading: The complement cascade
paragraphs.text: The complement system uses proteins to identify and destroy pathogens, and it also clears away dead and damaged cells. Once a pathogen gets past the epithelial barrier, complement proteins, soluble plasma proteins numbered C1 to C9, are activated and set off a chain of reactions that kill pathogens outside cells. In the classical pathway, an antibody bound to a pathogen lets C1 attach, which activates C4 and C2, and these combine into C3 convertase. C3 convertase then splits into C3a, which draws immune cells to the infection and boosts inflammation, and C3b, which helps build the membrane attack complex that breaks open the pathogen's membrane. The alternative pathway follows similar steps but begins when C3 activates on its own.
